content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The entry's core identification — that the Shadow of Death names the contrary pattern of sin, darkness, and bondage whose wages end in the grave, standing opposite the sheltering shadow of Christ — is carried well by the texts printed with it. Psalm 107:10,14 explicitly binds the shadow of death to darkness and literal bondage ('bound in affliction and iron... brake their bands in sunder'), which fits a condition/pattern reading better than a bare 'mortal peril' gloss. Isaiah 9:2 and Luke 1:78-79 present the shadow of death as a state people sit or dwell in, dispelled by the dayspring who guides 'into the way of peace' — a way-versus-way inversion that directly supports the entry's two-shadow structure. Romans 6:23 supplies the 'wages... end in the pit or grave' clause verbatim in substance, and Philippians 2:5-9 supplies Christ's way of living that leads through death into exaltation and life. The strongest counter — the mainstream reading of deep darkness/mortal peril — does not contradict the entry's core referent: mainstream interpretation itself (Response A) extends the phrase to the spiritual darkness and condition of humanity apart from God, dispelled by Christ's light. That counter is a broader, less articulated version of the same referent, not a rival identification, and it explains the bondage language of Ps 107 and the way-of-peace antithesis of Luke 1:79 less specifically than the entry does. No supplied text is inexplicable on the entry's core reading: Psalm 23:4's righteous traverser is walking through, not dwelling in, the domain, which the entry's shadow-as-outline mechanics handles without strain. Chapter-level applications (Colossians discharge polemic, annihilationism in ch. 16) are out of scope and do not diminish the printed entry.","book_core_identification":"The Shadow of Death is the contrary pattern (domain/way) of sin, darkness, and bondage — the inverse of the shadow of Christ — whose wages terminate in the pit or grave.","book_secondary_elaborations":["A shadow is an image, outline, or boundary of its subject (shadow-mechanics premise, supported by the tsel/tselem derivation and by shadows being attached to the bodies that cast them).","The Shadow of Christ (Shadow of Life) is defined in part by His appointed times, feasts, assemblies, and way of living (tracks Colossians 2:16-17, where holydays, new moons, and sabbaths are called 'a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ').","Christ's way of living leads through death into eternal life (supported by Philippians 2:5-9's descent-through-death-to-exaltation arc and Romans 6:23's 'gift of God is eternal life')."],"unsupported_glossary_assertions":[],"chapter_only_objections":["The chapter's claim that Colossians 2:16-17 protects rather than discharges feast-keeping, and the anti-supersessionist application, is a chapter-level argument not asserted in the entry.","The chapter's universal thesis that biblical 'shadow' always means shelter/defence must contend with the Job corpus and the philological case that tsalmaveth/tsalmut means simply 'deep darkness' with no death-compound; this affects the chapter's sweep, not the entry.","The tselem-from-tsel etymology (image built on shade-word) is a contested philological claim used as chapter evidence.","The Heaven and Hell chapter's annihilationist reading of Romans 6:23 and 'second death' material (acher maveth, Cochin manuscripts, Plato genealogy) is a separate doctrinal edifice not printed in this entry."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The traditional/critical mainstream reading: 'shadow of death' (tsalmaveth, or revocalized tsalmut, 'deep darkness') is a poetic figure for the deepest darkness and mortal peril — the looming threat or near presence of death — through which God accompanies His people (Ps 23:4), extended in the prophetic/NT strand (Isa 9:2; Matt 4:16; Luke 1:79) to the spiritual darkness and hopeless condition of humanity apart from God, dispelled by the light of Christ. It is an image of extremity and gloom, not a defined counter-pattern or systematic inverse of a 'Shadow of Christ.'","counter_core_identification":"The shadow of death is deepest darkness/mortal peril and, derivatively, the spiritual darkness of those without God's light — a figure of extremity rather than a structured contrary pattern of sin and bondage.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"SAME_CORE_BROADER","material_core_denial":"A true rival would have to assert that the phrase denotes only physical gloom or the proximity of physical death and denies any association with sin, bondage, or a condition dispelled by Christ. But even the mainstream account concedes the Isa 9:2/Luke 1:79 strand as spiritual darkness apart from God, so both identifications can be true of the same referent; the counter does not deny the book's core.","counter_case":["Psalm 23:4 most naturally depicts a righteous man in mortal danger, not a man inside a pattern of sin — the peril reading is simpler for that verse.","The philological consensus (tsalmut = 'deep darkness') and the Job usages (3:5; 10:21-22; 34:22) favor generic gloom or the realm of the dead over any moralized pattern.","The 'inverse of the Shadow of Christ' framing and the term 'Shadow of Life' appear nowhere verbatim in Scripture; the two-shadow system is a constructed schema.","Several shadow-of-death texts (Job, Amos 5:8) concern cosmic or atmospheric darkness with no sin/bondage context."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["Psalm 107:10-14 explicitly welds the shadow of death to bondage ('bound in affliction and iron') and deliverance ('brake their bands in sunder'), which the entry's darkness-and-bondage pattern predicts and the bare 'mortal peril' gloss must treat as incidental coloring.","Luke 1:79 opposes those sitting in the shadow of death to being guided 'into the way of peace' — a way-versus-way antithesis that directly supports the entry's contrary-pattern structure, with the dayspring (light/Christ) as the opposing term, exactly the inversion the entry names.","Romans 6:23, printed with the entry, supplies the causal chain sin → wages → death/grave versus gift → eternal life through Christ, giving the entry's final clause verse-level support and grounding the two-track inversion.","Philippians 2:5-9 supplies the 'way of living which leads through death into eternal life' for the opposite shadow: Christ's mind, obedience unto death, and exaltation.","The shadow-as-outline mechanics (a shadow implies a body and a light behind it; a shadow cannot kill) coherently explains why Psalm 23:4 says 'through' and why Isa 9:2/Ps 107:14/Amos 5:8 all pair the shadow of death with a light that dispels it — the counter treats the light-pairing as coincidence of imagery.","Colossians 2:16-17 textually lists appointed times as a shadow whose body 'is of Christ,' supporting the entry's definition of the opposite shadow without requiring the chapter's further polemic."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["Simpler handling of Psalm 23:4 as a righteous sufferer in deadly danger.","Better fit for the Job corpus and Amos 5:8 as generic deep darkness — though none of these are printed with the entry.","Requires no extra-biblical term ('Shadow of Life') or systematizing schema."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Psalm 107:10, 14 — shadow of death defined in context as darkness plus bondage, broken by God's deliverance","Luke 1:78-79 — those in the shadow of death guided by the dayspring into the way of peace: the light/way inversion the entry asserts","Romans 6:23 — wages of sin is death vs gift of eternal life through Christ, the entry's terminal clause and two-track structure","Isaiah 9:2 — dwelling in the land of the shadow of death, upon whom light shines","Philippians 2:5-9 — Christ's way through death into exaltation, the opposing pattern","Colossians 2:16-17 (via supporting chapter) — appointed times called shadow whose body is of Christ"],"unresolved_objections":["The philological question whether tsalmaveth is a true death-compound or a revocalized 'deep darkness' (tsalmut) remains open, though it does not defeat the entry, which builds on the canonical form and the LXX/NT skia thanatou tradition.","The label 'Shadow of Life' is the book's coinage rather than a scriptural phrase; the entry presents it as an interpretive equation, supported structurally but not verbally.","Job's non-moralized uses of the term are not addressed by the printed references, though they are also not cited by the entry."],"confidence":"medium"}
